clue.text: Unruly tribes in brown

indicators.note: unruly letters are out of control, so the word tribes is to be rearranged

parts.words: tribes

explanation.surface: Lawless tribesmen dressed in brown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unruly' rearranges TRIBES into the answer; 'in' just links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bistre is a brownish pigment made from soot, and so names a dark brown colour.

clue.text: Lavengro fan at the library ?

parts.words: Lavengro fan at the library
parts.note: Lavengro is a novel by George Borrow, so his fan could be called a ..., and at a library one takes out books

explanation.surface: An admirer of a Victorian novel visiting the library.
explanation.walkthrough: Lavengro (1851) is by George Borrow; a fan of his would be a 'Borrow-er', and a library user takes out books on loan.
explanation.definitionFit: A library user takes books out on loan, which makes them a lender's customer.

clue.text: " Along the cool vale of life" (Gray)

definitions.text: " Along the cool vale of life" (Gray)

parts.words: " Along the cool vale of life" (Gray)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard: the missing word describes the secluded valley

explanation.surface: A line of verse from Gray, with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Gray's Elegy: 'Along the cool ___ vale of life / They kept the noiseless tenor of their way.'
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a valley that is secluded and withdrawn from the world.

clue.text: Blue spirit

explanation.surface: Feeling low in mood, or a ghostly presence.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'blue' money is old British slang for squandering it; gin is nicknamed 'mother's ruin', so the word stands for the spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue as a verb means to waste or squander, wreck one's fortune; gin, the spirit, is nicknamed mother's ruin.

clue.text: What's new for the night-flier's companion?

definitions.text: What's new for the night-flier's companion?

parts.words: What's new for the night-flier's companion
parts.note: the night-flier is the owl of Lear's nonsense poem, whose companion went to sea with him; 'What's New ...' is the title of a well-known 1960s song addressed to that companion

explanation.surface: A question asking what news there is for a nocturnal bird's friend.
explanation.walkthrough: Two references meet: Edward Lear's 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat' gives the owl's companion, and the Tom Jones song 'What's New Pussycat?' gives the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: In Lear's nonsense verse the owl sails away with a cat, the friend of the night bird.

clue.text: Papal state ?

parts.words: Papal state
parts.note: a Papal State was a territory ruled by the Pope, but here it is the condition of being like Pope Urban

explanation.surface: A territory once ruled by the Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: Several popes were called Urban, so the condition of being one is read as 'Urban-ity'.
explanation.definitionFit: Urbanity is suave, courteous polish of manner.

clue.text: Where to take off in Devon

definitions.text: Where to take off in Devon

parts.words: Where to take off in Devon
parts.note: take off reads as setting out, but the place is a headland on the Devon coast

explanation.surface: A Devon airfield or launching spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Start Point is a headland on the south Devon coast, England; read as two words it is where one would begin.
explanation.definitionFit: A headland named as the place one begins, the spot to depart from.

clue.text: Its carrier takes the blame

parts.words: Its carrier takes the blame
parts.note: the idiom for accepting blame for others says one carries this container

explanation.surface: A remark that whoever bears something gets blamed.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'carry the can' is a British idiom for taking the blame.
explanation.definitionFit: A tin container is what the idiom about bearing responsibility says one carries.

clue.text: If music be the food of love, so are these' dates

definitions.text: If music be the food of love, so are these' dates

parts.words: If music be the food of love, so are these' dates
parts.note: Orsino's line from Twelfth Night is borrowed, and dates are both fruit and lovers' appointments

explanation.surface: Romantic meetings likened to Shakespeare's food of love.
explanation.walkthrough: Dates are a food (the fruit) as well as lovers' meetings, so they too are food of love.
explanation.definitionFit: Trysts are secret romantic meetings, lovers' assignations.

clue.text: "For the rain it raineth every day ", he sang

definitions.text: "For the rain it raineth every day ", he sang

parts.words: "For the rain it raineth every day ", he sang
parts.note: the refrain of the clown's closing song in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night

explanation.surface: A singer's gloomy refrain about constant rain.
explanation.walkthrough: The song closes Twelfth Night and is sung by Olivia's jester.
explanation.definitionFit: Feste is the jester in Twelfth Night who sings 'When that I was and a little tiny boy'.

clue.text: Repay when about to leave the Orient

parts.words: about
parts.note: re is Latin-derived 'about, concerning'

parts.words: to leave
parts.note: to quit is to leave

parts.words: the Orient
parts.note: E stands for east, the Orient

explanation.surface: Settling a debt as one quits the Far East.
explanation.definitionFit: To requite is to pay back or return a favour or injury in kind.

clue.text: The kiss is hard, but the soap is soft

definitions.text: The kiss is hard, but the soap is soft

parts.words: The kiss is hard, but the soap is soft
parts.note: the kiss is the awkward one given to a stone at an Irish castle, hanging backwards; soft soap is smooth flattery

explanation.surface: A remark contrasting a firm kiss with a gentle soap.
explanation.walkthrough: Kissing the Blarney Stone at Blarney Castle in Ireland is said to give the gift of the gab; the stone is hard, and the gift it gives is soft soap.
explanation.definitionFit: Blarney is flattering, persuasive talk, the soft-soaping eloquence the Irish stone is said to bestow.

clue.text: Nothing new on the return of Glendower

parts.words: Nothing
parts.note: O is the round figure nought

indicators.note: the return asks for the word new to be read backwards

parts.words: new
parts.note: taken as written; that 'new on' read backwards also holds the answer is a coincidence, since 'Nothing' must give its O

explanation.surface: A remark that Glendower's comeback brings nothing fresh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link word placing nought before the turned word. Glendower is Shakespeare's spelling of the Welsh leader's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Owen Glendower (Owain Glyndwr) was the Welsh rebel prince who appears in Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1.

clue.text: Provide grand entertainment at the races ?

definitions.text: Provide grand entertainment at the races ?

parts.words: Provide grand entertainment at the races
parts.note: the idiom for paying for everyone's food and drink is read as the grandstand at a racecourse laying on a treat

explanation.surface: Laying on a lavish spread for guests at a race meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grand' hints at the grandstand, the 'stand' at a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand treat is to pay for refreshments or entertainment for others.

clue.text: Hamlet's canon-fixer

parts.words: Hamlet's canon-fixer
parts.note: Hamlet wishes 'the ... had not fix'd His canon 'gainst self-slaughter', a canon being a law, not a gun

explanation.surface: Someone in Hamlet who fixed a cannon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'canon' looks like a gun; it is a church law, which God fixed against suicide in Hamlet's first soliloquy.
explanation.definitionFit: God is called the Everlasting, the eternal one, in Hamlet's speech.

clue.text: War histories of the scissors-and-paste kind ?

definitions.text: War histories of the scissors-and-paste kind ?

parts.words: War histories of the scissors-and-paste kind
parts.note: a scrap is a fight, so books of scraps could be war histories, though really they hold pasted cuttings

explanation.surface: Military histories cobbled together from other works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' means a fight in British slang, so these could be books about scraps.
explanation.definitionFit: Albums of pasted cuttings and pictures are made with scissors and glue.

clue.text: Tempt with a yorker ?

parts.words: Tempt with a yorker
parts.note: in old cricket slang a tice is a yorker, a ball pitched at the batsman's feet to lure a stroke; 'en' read as 'with' or 'in' puts one in front

explanation.surface: Luring a batsman with a ball aimed at the toes.
explanation.walkthrough: A yorker in cricket is a delivery that pitches right at the batsman's feet; an older name for it was a 'tice', from the same root as the answer, since it entices the batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: To entice is to tempt or lure, exactly what a tice does to a batsman.

clue.text: Blows welcomed by Kitty

explanation.surface: Kitty receiving her punches with pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: Kitty is a cat here, not a woman: a cat welcomes being petted.
explanation.definitionFit: Strokes are blows or hits, and also the gentle caresses a cat enjoys.

clue.text: Ecclesiastical offering that is somewhat dating

definitions.text: Ecclesiastical offering that is somewhat dating

parts.words: Ecclesiastical offering that is somewhat dating
parts.note: the church offering splits into an alteration of age, as something that dates one does

explanation.surface: A church donation that seems rather old-fashioned.
explanation.walkthrough: The word sounds like 'alter age', changing one's age, which 'dating' suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Altarage was the offering made at a church altar, or the priest's income from such gifts.

clue.text: Haydn's music in the making!

parts.words: Haydn's music in the making
parts.note: Haydn's oratorio title, and also the act of making something

explanation.surface: A Haydn piece being composed.
explanation.walkthrough: Haydn wrote an oratorio called The Creation; the word also means making something.
explanation.definitionFit: Creation is the act of bringing something into being, and Haydn's oratorio of that title.

clue.text: Crumby like the accompaniment to chips ?

definitions.text: Crumby like the accompaniment to chips ?

parts.words: Crumby like the accompaniment to chips
parts.note: the partner of chips is fish, which can be fried, and the word for crumbling sounds like 'fry-able'

explanation.surface: Something crumbly, rather like the fish served with chips.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sounds like 'fry-able', which is what the fish beside the chips must be; its true sense is easily crumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: Friable means easily crumbled, as crumbly soil or pastry is.

clue.text: Playing hooky is a serious matter to him

definitions.text: Playing hooky is a serious matter to him

parts.words: Playing hooky is a serious matter to him
parts.note: playing hooky usually means truancy, but here it is playing a hooked fish on the line

explanation.surface: Someone who takes truancy very seriously.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing hooky' reads as skipping school, but this person plays a fish caught on a hook.
explanation.definitionFit: An angler fishes with rod and line, playing each hooked fish to land it.

clue.text: " There is a willow grows — a brook " (Hamlet)

definitions.text: " There is a willow grows — a brook " (Hamlet)

parts.words: " There is a willow grows — a brook " (Hamlet)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Gertrude's report of Ophelia's drowning in Hamlet

explanation.surface: A line from Hamlet with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Gertrude's line is 'There is a willow grows aslant a brook'.
explanation.definitionFit: The willow leans at an angle across the stream, slanting over it.

clue.text: Change of abode

indicators.note: a change of letters asks for the word abode to be rearranged

parts.words: abode

explanation.surface: Moving house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change of' rearranges ABODE; the whole clue also defines, since an adobe is a dwelling.
explanation.definitionFit: An adobe is a house built of sun-dried clay bricks, a different kind of dwelling.

clue.text: Facial decorations that are very dishy!

explanation.surface: Whiskers that make their wearer very attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dishy' means attractive in British slang, but here it means holding dishes: a sideboard is dining-room furniture for crockery. In Britain sideboards also means sideburns.
explanation.definitionFit: Sideburns are whiskers on the cheeks, and a dresser storing plates is a piece of dish-laden furniture.

clue.text: Juno type with oomph is mountainous

definitions.note: an adjective in the clue for a noun, a mountain

parts.words: Juno type
parts.note: a statuesque Junoesque woman is outsize, abbreviated OS

parts.words: oomph
parts.note: SA, sex appeal, is oomph

explanation.surface: A goddess-like woman full of vigour is huge.
explanation.walkthrough: OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize, fitting a large Junoesque figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Ossa is a mountain in Thessaly, Greece, famed in myth for being piled on Pelion.

clue.text: It ran down to a sunless sea

definitions.text: It ran down to a sunless sea

parts.words: It ran down to a sunless sea
parts.note: Coleridge's Kubla Khan: 'Where the sacred river ran ... Down to a sunless sea'

explanation.surface: Something that flowed into a dark ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: In Kubla Khan, Coleridge names the sacred river of Xanadu.
explanation.definitionFit: Alph is the sacred river of Xanadu in Coleridge's poem.

clue.text: Not that it introduced a jarring note at a Lucullan feast!

definitions.text: Not that it introduced a jarring note at a Lucullan feast

parts.words: Not that it introduced a jarring note at a Lucullan feast
parts.note: a jarring note is normally a discordant element, but here it is a jar, the Roman wine vessel, served at a lavish banquet like those of the general Lucullus

explanation.surface: Insisting nothing struck a discordant note at a sumptuous banquet.
explanation.walkthrough: Lucullus was a Roman famous for lavish feasts; the 'jarring' item there was a two-handled jar of wine.
explanation.definitionFit: An amphora is a tall two-handled ancient jar for wine or oil.

clue.text: The Colonel cannot beat 'it of course!

definitions.text: The Colonel cannot beat 'it of course

parts.words: The Colonel cannot beat 'it of course
parts.note: Colonel Bogey is the golfer's imaginary opponent, and on a golf course the standard score is hard to beat

explanation.surface: A military man admits he cannot win, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like 'naturally', but means on the golf course. Colonel Bogey is golf's notional player; bogey and the standard score are close.
explanation.definitionFit: Par is the standard number of strokes for a golf hole, the score to beat.

clue.text: Painter musician

explanation.surface: An artist who also makes music.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Bellini was a Venetian painter; Vincenzo Bellini an Italian opera composer.

clue.text: He doesn't take chaff lightly

parts.words: He doesn't take chaff lightly
parts.note: chaff here is not teasing banter but husks beaten from grain, which this worker strikes hard

explanation.surface: A man who resents being teased.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chaff' looks like banter; it is the husk separated from grain by beating.
explanation.definitionFit: A thresher beats harvested grain to separate it from the chaff.

clue.text: Feudal big noise apt to make a display of force ?

definitions.text: Feudal big noise apt to make a display of force ?

parts.words: Feudal big noise apt to make a display of force
parts.note: a big noise is an important person in feudal Japan, and the title splits into words suggesting showing a firearm

explanation.surface: A powerful lord inclined to flex his muscles.
explanation.walkthrough: The title sounds like 'show gun', a display of force.
explanation.definitionFit: A shogun was the hereditary military ruler of feudal Japan.
